title: Quantification of the carbon content of single grains in martensite-ferrite dual phase steel by UHV-EDXS
abstract: The detection and quantification of carbon by conventional energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS) performed under standard conditions is not feasible due to occurring contaminations in common electron microscopes. In contrast, novel ultra high vacuum EDXS (UHV-EDXS) was used to acquire elemental mappings of carbon on dual phase (DP) steel, which exhibits a microstructure consisting of ferrite and martensite. These phases differ in hardness, local dislocation density and, most importantly, in their carbon content. Since the UHV conditions in combination with a customized windowless EDXS detector ensured a minimization of hydrocarbon contamination during the measurements and a maximization of the sensitivity for the detection of light elements, UHV-EDXS carbon mappings could successfully be obtained, which clearly reflect the ferrite and martensite microstructure of the investigated DP steels, as confirmed by electron back scatter diffraction (EBSD). Most importantly, it was possible to quantify the carbon content of individual grains with concentrations as low as 0.25 wt%. Furthermore, nano-hardness tests were performed on the very same grains which were characterized by UHV-EDXS and EBSD. It is shown that the hardness of the martensite grains is correlated to their carbon content, as directly determined by UHV-EDXS. With this new method an additional tool for advanced material characterization of multiphase materials on the level of individual grains is now available.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In the automotive industry advanced high strength steels (AHSS) are of increasing importance, with dual phase (DP) steel being in the focus for safety related structures exhibiting high potential of energy absorption [ 1–7 ]. The combination of two different phases in DP steels, namely martensite and ferrite, leads to a complex material, with the macroscopic properties being mainly dependent on the martensite volume fraction (MVF) as well as on the carbon (C) content of the martensite phase [ 6 , 8 ]. DP steels with high MVF, as considered in this work, can exhibit high tensile strengths up to 800–1200 MPa [ 9–11 ].

The specific heat treatment applied for a DP steel substantially influences the properties of the material, since the microstructure is determined by the annealing temperature as well as annealing time as steering parameters. In general, cooling of the steel from high temperatures down to below the critical transformation temperature  A 
                      
                         c 3  results in a phase transition of the face centered cubic (fcc) structure of austenite ( γ -Fe) into ferrite ( α -Fe), which is an equilibrium phase with a body centered cubic (bcc) lattice. Since the maximum solubility of C in ferrite is very low with only 0.02 wt%, excess C diffuses out of the grains, rendering ferrite soft and easily deformable. Martensite, which is a metastable state ( α ’-Fe), is obtained by rapid cooling of the austenite material below the martensite start temperature with cooling rates higher than the critical one. Contrary to the phase transition of austenite into ferrite, the diffusion of the C out of the grains is prevented. Consequently, the C within the parent austenite grains stays dissolved in the formed martensite and gives rise to high residual stress and a high local dislocation density [ 12–14 ], resulting in a material with high hardness and strength.

A combination of the two phases is present in DP steel which can be obtained by cooling the austenite down from a temperature above  A 
                      
                         c 3 , annealing it at a temperature in the ferrite and austenite ( α  +  γ ) phase field, and by subsequently cooling the material further down so that the remaining austenite transforms into martensite, a process which is known as step quenching [ 15–17 ]. By varying the annealing temperature and time it is firstly possible to change the MVF and therefore also the overall tensile strength of the DP steel [ 8 , 18 ]. Secondly, also the tensile strength of the martensite itself, which is related to the C content in this phase, has an impact on the mechanical properties of the material [ 8 ].

Depending on the considered length scale, the evaluation of the microstructure in optical micrographs or by electron back scatter diffraction (EBSD) are commonly used for distinguishing the different phases and to determine the MVF in DP steels [ 6 , 12 ]. Since both martensite and ferrite show a similar crystal structure [ 19 ], for EBSD the high residual stress and high local dislocation density in martensite is used by quantifying the corresponding band contrast (BC) or band slope contrast (BS) of the diffraction patterns [ 12–14 , 20–22 ].

With respect to the (local) determination of the C content in the martensite phase electron energy loss spectroscopy and secondary ion mass spectrometry can be found as used methods in literature [ 23 , 24 ]. Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS) to directly measure the elemental concentration of the individual phases seems an equally promising technique. However, measurements of light elements, like C, with EDXS prove to be difficult, since their X-ray signals are re-absorbed easier than those of heavier atoms. At the same time the fluorescence yield for low atomic numbers Z is small. Additionally, (carbon) contamination of the sample will hamper a meaningful quantification. In this context not only the contamination of the sample itself is detrimental, also the electron beam inside the chamber of a scanning electron microscope (SEM) usually induces significant contaminations on the investigated areas due to the residual gas in the high vacuum [ 25 ].

In order to cope with the above adressed issues for the detection of light elements and especially of C by EDXS it is necessary to provide a suitable experimental environment for reliable material characterization. Consequently, in this work it is shown for the first time to the best of our knowledge that ultra high vacuum energy dispersive X-Ray spectroscopy (UHV-EDXS) is capable to directly measure and quantify the C content exemplified for the individual phases and even for single grains in DP steels. Moreover, it is proven that the hardness of the martensite grains in DP steel is correlated with their C content. For that purpose and for a direct comparison, nanoindention, EDXS as well as EBSD measurements were performed in the very same area of DP steel samples with varying MVF.

sections.heading: Sample material
paragraphs:
Five different samples were used in this study. While all samples have the same overall chemical composition of a maximum of 0.23 wt% C, 1.00 wt% Si, 2.9 wt% Mn, 1.4 wt% Cr + Mo and 1.00 wt% Al the heat treatment for each sample varied. The corresponding annealing temperatures and times are shown in  Fig. 1 
                         , which represent typical parameters for current developments of DP steel material in industry. The cold rolled steel specimens were austenitized at 850 °C for 180 s and then cooled down at 75 K/s by gas jet cooling to a certain annealing temperature. As seen in  Fig. 1 , the annealing temperatures were between 625 and 700 °C, the annealing times between 400 and 1800 s. The austenite transforms into ferrite, with the transformation being accelerated for lower temperatures. This implies that the ferrite volume fraction is not only dependent on the annealing time but also on the annealing temperature. After a specific time the samples were quenched to room temperature and the remaining austenite phase transforms into martensite, resulting in a steel, which possesses a dual phase microstructure consisting of martensite and ferrite. One of the samples was cooled down immediately without additional annealing step so that it consists only of martensite. The amount of retained austenite was equal or less than 3% for all samples, as determined by dilatometry measurements.

Prior to the analysis the samples were polished with an active oxide suspension (OP-S), additionally Ar-ion polished at 4 kV for 30 min and at 1 kV for 2 h, with the incident angle of the ion beams at 6° with respect to the surface, and finally cleaned in an ultrasonic bath with tetrahydrofuran, isopropanol and ethanol for 15 min, each step carried out for two consecutive times. Finally, the samples were sputtered with Ar-ions inside the UHV chamber of the used Auger electron microscope for a short time to further decrease any carbon deposition on the surface and to remove the surface oxide layer before the EDXS measurements were performed.

For a direct comparison and correlation of the hardness measurements by nanoindentation with the EDXS mappings as well as with the EBSD measurements, an area of 100  μ m x 100  μ m was marked with indents on each sample prior analysis.

sections.heading: Analytical methods
paragraphs: The EDXS measurements were performed in a scanning Auger electron microscope JAMP 9500F (Jeol, Japan). The system is equipped with a hemispherical electron energy analyzer enabling spectroscopic Auger electron measurements as well as with an Ar-ion sputter gun. The ion energies can be varied between 0 and 3 keV, which can be used for sputter depth profiling or sputter cleaning of the samples. Most importantly for this work, the system is equipped with a windowless EDX Ultim Max detector custom designed for UHV-operation (Oxford Instruments, UK). The pressure of the UHV chamber is <10 −7  Pa, so that ideal conditions for the measurement of light elements with the windowless EDXS-detector are met. The EDXS measurements were performed at a working distance of 24 mm and at a rather low acceleration voltage of 5 kV to provide a shallow excitation volume in order to facilitate the detection of the low energy characteristic X-rays of light elements which are prone to high absorption. The EDXS mappings covered a region of 143  μ m x 107  μ m with a resolution of 1024 × 764 pixels. The Aztec software from Oxford Instruments, which was used for controlling and evaluating the data, has a fixed set of process times. For the measurements a setting for the process time of 4 was used. The dwell time per pixel was 30 ms, resulting in relatively long measurement times of up to 11 h per map. The dead time was 43–47%, due to maximization of the output count rate. The total counts per mapping resulted in over 2 ∗ 10 9  counts. For the quantification the standard set for 5 kV provided by Oxford Instruments was used. The results were normalized and the threshold was set to three sigma.

Additionally, EBSD measurements were performed at 20 kV with a Jeol JSM-7800F SEM equipped with a Symmetry EBSD detector from Oxford Instruments. The chosen working distance was 17 mm, the step size for the EBSD mappings was set to 100 nm.
The hardness tests were carried out with a Nanoflip50 nanoindentor (Nanomechanics, USA) installed in an Ultra 55 SEM (Zeiss, Germany). The target load was in all measurements 5 mN.

sections.heading: EBSD
paragraphs:
The DP steel samples were at first characterized by EBSD to obtain information about the microstructure and the MVF on the same length scale as the subsequent characterization by UHV-EDXS. For EBSD, the BS contrast mappings for the bcc crystal structure of all five samples are shown in  Fig. 2 
                         . The martensite and ferrite grains of the DP steel can be distinguished by the brightness level of the BS contrast, since the EBSD quality, which is quantified by the BC or BS, is different for the two phases [ 12–14 , 20–22 ]. The formation of martensite results in a large number of dislocations and high residual strain leading to a lower quality of the EBSD pattern. Thus, ferrite has a higher BS value and a brighter colour than martensite in the mappings, which was used to determine the MVF of the sample material [ 13 , 14 , 20–22 ]. For the considered set of samples, the MVF decreases with decreasing annealing temperature and larger areas with grains of ferrite are formed, as shown in the inset and the magnified view of  Fig. 2  e).

sections.heading: Chemical composition and mapping of elements
paragraphs:
In  Fig. 3 
                             the EDX mappings of C for all five samples are depicted, together with the Fe and Mn mappings of the sample annealed at 625 °C for comparison. As for all samples, Fe and Mn show a rather uniform distribution, beside minor Mn segregations in form of stripes within the scanned area. C is also homogeneously distributed in the mapping of  Fig. 3  a) for the sample, which consist only of martensite. In contrast, an inhomogeneous distribution of C is observed for the mappings depicted in  Fig. 3  b)–e). A comparison with  Fig. 2  shows that this distribution ressembles the one of martensite, with the martensite being brighter in colour in the C mapping and darker in colour in the BS mapping. To ensure that the C concentration differences do not originate from channeling effects of differently oriented grains, the measurements were repeated for one of the samples with the stage slightly tilted to different angles, which lead to comparable results.

The sum spectra obtained from the individual mappings look nearly identical for all of the samples, since they exhibit the same overall chemical composition. Thus, in  Fig. 4 
                             the EDXS sum spectrum and the evaluated concentrations for the detected elements from only one of the mapped areas are shown as example. Since the element of interest is C in this study, a low accelerating voltage is preferred, which also lowers the accuracy of the measurement for heavier elements. Unfortunately, the Cr and Mn peaks overlap with one of the Fe peaks, making an accurate quantification difficult. Furthermore, it can be noticed that the directly obtained concentration for C with 1.7 wt% is far too high for DP steels. This discrepancy is attributed, besides potential inaccuracies in the used standards and background substraction routine, to residual C contaminations of the samples or even of the detector unit, which cannot be ruled out despite the prevailing UHV conditions. Nevertheless, in the case of DP steel, a straightforward approach can be applied for a reliable C quantification, as detailed in the following.

sections.heading: Carbon content of the different phases
paragraphs:
While for the diffusive phase transformation of austenite into ferrite the carbon partitions into the remaining austenitic phase, this carbon enriched austenite transforms then diffusionless into martensite upon cooling to room temperature. The resulting martensite is therefore supersaturated in C. The EDXS mappings of C confirm this picture, together with the information obtained by EBSD. As presented in  Section 3.1  the ferrite and martensite phases were identified by their BS value, which can now be used to assign the C content of single grains to the corresponding phase. In  Fig. 5 
                             such a direct comparison is shown as an example for the sample annealed at 625 °C, with individual grains visible in the EBSD and C mappings, as well as in the secondary electron image.

To compare the four samples, which have a microstructure containing both, martensite and ferrite with varying MVF, 12–15 grains were randomly selected per mapped area, as  e.g.  indicated for the sample in  Fig. 5 .

The EDXS spectra of these grains were then extracted from the mappings and evaluated with respect to their C content. The C content for ferrite and martensite obtained in this way for the four samples is given in  Fig. 6 
                             a). At first, one can observe that the standard deviation for measurements in the ferrite phase is rather high. However, because of the extended interaction volume of the electron beam it is possible that X-ray signals from martensite underneath or next to the ferrite grain of interest are added to the spectrum. For measurements in the martensite region, nanoscale iron carbides (Fe 3 C) may also contribute to the spectra, resulting in a varying C content for the individual grains. As to the absolute concentration of C, one can take advantage of the fact that the maximum solubility of C in ferrite is negligible with only 0.02 wt%, in contrast to the obtained average concentration of 1.5 wt% given in  Fig. 6  a). Consequently, this phase can now be used as internal reference for the determination of the C content in the martensite phase. With the excess value from the ferrite phase subtracted as an offset from the concentration of martensite, a clear trend shows up, as depicted in  Fig. 6  b). With increasing MVF the carbon content in the grains reduces as expected. Under the above mentioned assumption that no C is dissolved in the ferrite phase the concentration of C in the overall DP bulk material can be derived as the martensite fraction multiplied with the mean value of the concentration of C in the martensite grains. This mean value of the concentration for C in all samples then results in 0.21 ± 0.01 wt% as measured by EDXS, closely matching the nominal C concentration of 0.23 wt% given for this type of DP steel.

sections.heading: Hardness of the grains measured by nanoindentation
paragraphs:
On all of the individual grains characterized by EBSD and EDXS a hardness test by nanoindentation was performed. The indents can be seen in  Fig. 7 
                          in the backscatter electron images of the five samples. The individual grains exhibit a different brightness and can also be distinguished by their form. The origin of the contrast can have various reasons, such as orientation effects. Consequently, the electron images give no clear indication whether the grains are martensite or ferrite ones. Nevertheless, it can be observed that some indents are significantly smaller than others. Since martensite is expected to be harder than ferrite the indentations should be shallower for martensite. By directly comparing the electron images with the BS images (see  Fig. 2 ) it is possible to identify whether the tested grain is of martensite or ferrite type and by additionally evaluating the EDXS spectrum a correlation between the C-content of the martensite and the hardness can be obtained. In  Fig. 7  e) such a direct comparison between the three mapping types for a small area is depicted as an example. The marked martensite grain seems to be slightly brighter than the ferrite one in the electron backscatter image, has a low BS contrast and a higher C content compared to the adjacent ferrite grain.

The hardness for the different phases and samples is summarized in  Fig. 8 
                         . Despite a larger experimental spread for the lower annealing temperatures and with a small deviation for the 650 °C sample, it is evident that the hardness of the martensite grains decreases with increasing MVF, while the hardness of the ferrite grains slightly increases. The increase of hardness in ferrite grains with increasing MVF has been reported before [ 6 , 26 , 27 ]. One possible explanation is related to the increased probability of the presence of martensite directly underneath the measured ferrite grains. Also the decrease of the hardness of martensite grains for increasing MVF fits to the overall behaviour of this material system, as reported before [ 6 , 27 , 28 ]. However, we could now confirm that the change in hardness is directly linked to the carbon content in the martensite phase, as determined by UHV-EDXS and depicted in  Fig. 8  b).

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: EDXS carried out with a customized windowless X-ray detector under UHV conditions was successfully used for the determination and even quantification of small differences in the C content of individual martensite grains in DP steels with varying MVF. Consequently, a direct and highly lateral resolved comparison of data obtained by UHV-EDXS, EBSD and nanoindentation could be obtained. In this way it was confirmed for the first time on the level of single grains that the hardness of the martensite phase in DP steel is decreasing for higher MVF, due to the simultaneously decreasing concentration in C.

Due to the novelty of UHV-EDXS, there are still open questions related to the use of reliable standards as well as to measurement and evaluation inaccuracies, especially for low concentrations of light elements. The occurrence of residual contaminations even under UHV conditions and the final achievable limits of this method have to be equally further studied in the future. Nevertheless, UHV-EDXS has been now introduced as a complementary and promising technique for advanced material characterization of multiphase materials on the level of individual grains.
